clue.text: Europeans use a box, having nails scattered around

indicators.note: the jumbled nails go around the next pieces, holding them inside
nails scattered about land in a new order, so the word nails is jumbled

parts.note: the box is slang for the television, TV

explanation.surface: Someone from Europe makes a crate, with nails strewn about the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scattered' gives LIANS here. 'box' is British slang for the television set.
explanation.definitionFit: People of Latvia, a Baltic state, are inhabitants of Europe.

clue.text: Crazy thing to put before one's coaches!

definitions.text: thing to put before one's coaches!
definitions.meaning: a locomotive, or ... for short, is the engine at the front of railway carriages

explanation.surface: An absurd idea about putting the cart before the horse with one's railway carriages.
explanation.definitionFit: Loco is US slang for mad and short for locomotive, the engine pulling coaches.

clue.text: Carrier using river flowing into Scottish waterway

indicators.note: the river letter runs into the Scottish one, ending up inside it

parts.note: the Tay is Scotland's longest river

explanation.surface: A boat using a river that joins a Scottish waterway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flowing into' puts R inside TAY.
explanation.definitionFit: A tray is a flat holder for carrying plates or drinks.

clue.text: European antelope, one caught to north and south

indicators.note: the antelope goes between the two copies, so it is held within them
in a down clue the same pair of letters sits both above and below, so it appears twice

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
the eland is a large African antelope

explanation.surface: A European antelope with one trapped above and below it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'north and south' gives IC twice, one above and one below ELAND in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Icelandic describes something from Iceland, a European nation.

clue.text: Somehow call Soane (sic) for description of his architecture

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An instruction to name the architect Soane, misspelling and all, to describe his buildings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somehow' rearranges CALL SOANE SIC. Sir John Soane was a Georgian architect working in the classical revival.
explanation.definitionFit: Soane's style revived Greek and Roman forms, which is the classical revival style.

clue.text: Expedition fixed by a female in enveloping garment

indicators.note: the garment wraps around the following letters, holding them within

parts.note: a sari is a draped Indian garment

explanation.surface: A trip arranged by a woman wearing a wraparound robe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enveloping' puts A and F inside SARI.
explanation.definitionFit: A safari is a journey, especially an organised trip to watch or hunt wildlife.

clue.text: Turn in silver objects originally in abundance

indicators.note: the go word sits inside the silver-plus-object letters

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
a go is a turn in a game

indicators.note: originally picks the first letter of objects

explanation.surface: Taking a turn among silver items, at first in plenty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts GO inside AGO, right after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: A gogo means in plenty, galore, as in 'drinks a gogo'.

clue.text: A jolly ancient teacher's final battle!

parts.note: a jolly is slang for a Royal Marine, RM
aged means very old
a don is a university teacher; the 's stands for is

explanation.surface: An old marine teacher's last fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' is old naval slang for a Royal Marine.
explanation.definitionFit: Armageddon is the last battle between good and evil foretold in Revelation.

clue.text: Prevailing worry over monarch regularly taking protein

parts.note: in means fashionable, prevailing

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the worry word is read backwards

parts.note: to fret is to worry
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen
being on a drug means taking it regularly

explanation.surface: A dominant anxiety about a king who keeps taking a protein supplement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns FRET into TERF. 'regularly' looks like an alternate-letter signal on monarch but goes with 'taking' to give ON.
explanation.definitionFit: Interferon is a protein the body releases to fight viruses.

clue.text: Escort taking tea with Argentinian statesman

parts.note: cha is an informal word for tea
Juan Perón was president of Argentina

explanation.surface: A bodyguard having a cuppa with an Argentine leader.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaperon accompanies and supervises someone, acting as an escort.

clue.text: Keep accepting graduate's layout of data

indicators.note: the castle word takes in the following letters, holding them inside

parts.note: a keep is the stronghold of a castle, a fort
an MA, Master of Arts, is a graduate

explanation.surface: An instruction to keep taking on graduates, with a mention of data layout.
explanation.walkthrough: Keep reads as a verb but is the noun for a castle stronghold.
explanation.definitionFit: A format is the arrangement or structure in which data is organised.

clue.text: Plant identified in mathematician's language?

parts.note: an adder is one who adds, a whimsical name for a mathematician, with the 's kept
a tongue is a language

explanation.surface: A flower whose name hides in a mathematician's jargon.
explanation.walkthrough: A snake's tongue is suggested, but the adder here is someone doing sums.
explanation.definitionFit: Adder's tongue is a small fern with a single spike resembling a snake's tongue.

clue.text: Minstrel died in dance, surrounded by retired engineers

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance

indicators.note: the letter for died goes into the word for surrounded by

parts.note: among means in the midst of, surrounded by

indicators.note: retired means gone back, so the engineers' letters are read backwards

parts.note: RE stands for Royal Engineers, the British Army corps

explanation.surface: A singer dropped dead at a dance, with a group of engineers around him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surrounded by' looks like a container signal but is a plain synonym; 'in' is the real one, giving ADMONG, and 'retired' reverses the Royal Engineers.
explanation.definitionFit: A balladmonger was a seller or singer of ballads, a kind of minstrel.

clue.text: Big blow involving rating for slapstick

indicators.note: involving means taking in, so the rating's letters go inside

parts.note: a knockout is a blow that floors an opponent
an AB, able seaman, is a naval rating

explanation.surface: A huge punch to a sailor makes for physical comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: A rating is a non-commissioned sailor, and an able seaman is the classic crossword example.
explanation.definitionFit: Knockabout comedy is boisterous physical farce, like slapstick.

clue.text: Stealing around Italian piazza initially splitting hairs

indicators.note: the stealing word goes around the following letters

parts.note: nicking is British slang for stealing

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of piazza

explanation.surface: Pickpocketing around an Italian square, then quibbling about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' wraps the stealing word round the inserted letters, which go in just after its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitpicking is fussy fault-finding over trivial details, like quibbling over tiny points.

clue.text: Semi-divine spirit reported near a pond, ultimately

indicators.note: reported means the words are spoken, so we use how they sound

parts.note: near means nigh, close by

indicators.note: ultimately points at the final letter of pond

explanation.surface: A nature spirit heard about close to a pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reported' turns 'nigh a' into NAIA by sound; 'ultimately' takes D from pond.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth a naiad is a water nymph, a minor goddess of springs and rivers.

clue.text: Push off parasitic fly trapped in part of tack

indicators.note: the insect is caught inside the riding-gear word

parts.note: tack is horse-riding equipment, of which the saddle is one part
the ked is a wingless fly that lives on sheep

explanation.surface: A rider told to go away after a bloodsucking fly gets caught in the saddle.
explanation.walkthrough: Tack is the riding gear of a horse: saddle, bridle and so on.
explanation.definitionFit: To push off is to leave quickly, and skedaddle is a slangy way to say clear off.

clue.text: A second individual transfixed by current smear

indicators.note: transfixed means pierced, so the current letter runs through the individual word

parts.note: a person is an individual
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: Someone electrocuted for a moment, and then a slur.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transfixed by' puts I inside PERSON.
explanation.definitionFit: An aspersion is a damaging remark, a slur on someone's reputation.

clue.text: Top university features monks or monkeys

parts.note: a cap is a top or lid
chins are facial features

explanation.surface: A leading university has either friars or apes on its staff.
explanation.definitionFit: Capuchins are both Franciscan friars and South American monkeys named after their hooded look.

clue.text: Guarding house, pug's first to snap

indicators.note: the outer letters protect the house abbreviation by surrounding it
first picks the opening letter of pug's

explanation.surface: A dog watching over its home is the first to bite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'snap' reads as the dog's bite but is the definition, a snapshot.
explanation.definitionFit: A snap is a casual photograph, a snapshot.

clue.text: Cad Harry once roughed up in a church office

indicators.note: roughed up means knocked about, so these letters are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: A cad named Harry was once beaten up in a church building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roughed up' rearranges CAD HARRY ONCE; the office is reached through the link 'in a'.
explanation.definitionFit: An archdeaconry is the rank and jurisdiction of an archdeacon, a senior Church post.

clue.text: Military activity that's possibly a bit boring?

definitions.meaning: a tool bit that bores holes

explanation.surface: A soldier's complaint that parade practice is rather dull.
explanation.definitionFit: Parade-ground practice for soldiers shares its name with the tool whose bit bores holes.

clue.text: Short-tailed bird endlessly climbing S African mountain

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing reads upwards, so the letters go backwards
endlessly drops the final letter of the bird

parts.note: the grebe is a diving bird with a stubby tail

explanation.surface: A stumpy-tailed bird keeps climbing a South African peak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' makes GREBE into GREB; 'climbing' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: Berg is the Afrikaans word for mountain, as in the Drakensberg range.

clue.text: One who employs solver and setter with little hesitation

parts.note: the two of them together are us
er is a brief hesitant sound

explanation.surface: An employer pauses to address both the puzzler and the puzzle compiler.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who employs a thing makes use of it, a consumer.

clue.text: Source of old equipment at home

parts.note: a rig is a set of equipment
in means at home, as in 'staying in'

explanation.surface: Where antique gear kept in the house came from.
explanation.definitionFit: A source is where something starts, its beginning or provenance.

clue.text: Result of wrinkles in faces? Not at first

definitions.text: Result of wrinkles in faces? Not at first

parts.words: Result of wrinkles in faces? Not at first
parts.note: lined skin is cruelly thought unattractive, but young unlined faces are not, so the plainness comes only later

explanation.surface: A wry remark that ageing faces lose their looks, though not straight away.
explanation.definitionFit: Plainness of looks is what wrinkles are unkindly said to produce as a face ages.

clue.text: Fastener, say, secured when retreating across lake

indicators.note: the reversed letters span the lake letter, holding it near the end
retreating means going backwards, so the say and secured letters are read in reverse

parts.note: eg, for example, means say
got means obtained, secured

explanation.surface: A clasp, for instance, made fast while backing away over a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when retreating' turns EG GOT into TOGGE; 'across' then puts L inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A toggle is a short bar pushed through a loop, used to fasten a coat.

clue.text: Youngster's support an ungrateful princess rejected

parts.note: a tee supports a golf ball

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the princess's name is read backwards

parts.note: Regan is one of King Lear's ungrateful daughters

explanation.surface: A young person stands by a thankless royal daughter who was cast off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns REGAN into NAGER.
explanation.definitionFit: A teenager is a youngster aged thirteen to nineteen.
